teaser.text: Paychex helps employers pay workers and carry the administrative burden of employment. Its business becomes clear when you follow one dollar from the employer, through payroll and related services, to the people and institutions who must receive it—and to Paychex’s own revenue.

blocks.heading: Where could Paychex's shares be by 2029?

paragraphs.text: The forecast's weighted path is modestly positive, but the outcomes spread widely by 2029. The weighted price is $110.58 in October 2027, a 3% return including dividends. It reaches $118.31 in October 2028, a 15% return. By October 2029, it reaches $127.21, a 28% return. The 2029 outcomes run from $77.30 in the bear case to $177.91 in the bull case, against today's $111.63.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for Paychex?

paragraphs.text: Earnings recover gradually in the base case. Revenue is $7,030 million in October 2027 and $7,420 million in October 2028. It reaches $7,840 million in October 2029, as pricing, added services, and Paycor synergies offset subdued payroll activity. Net margins rise from 27.7% to 28.2%, then reach 28.7%, allowing earnings to move from $1,947 million to $2,249 million. The path reflects 5%–6% revenue guidance and 7%–9% adjusted EPS guidance, alongside FY2026 adjusted net income of $1,984.8 million and more than $100 million of reported synergies.

The bear case uses revenue of $6,890 million in 2027 and $7,130 million in 2028. It reaches $7,380 million in 2029. Margins fall from 25.5% to 24.5%, then 24.0%, as insurance costs, interest, and weak operating leverage reduce earnings. The bull case reaches $7,160 million in 2027 and $7,640 million in 2028, then $8,175 million in 2029. Margins rise from 28.8% to 29.5%, then 30.0%, because cross-selling and productivity gains prove durable.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Paychex really make?

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow means operating cash flow after capital spending, including internally developed software. Payroll processing needs less physical infrastructure than manufacturing, but software remains a real cash requirement. Cash flow also exceeds net income when amortization and other noncash expenses reduce profit without requiring another payment in the current year.

Stock compensation needs a separate lens. Employees receive value, while shareholders bear dilution, so deducting stock pay from free cash flow is a useful analytical allowance even though it is not another bank payment.

blocks.heading: How much does Paychex pay in dividends?

paragraphs.text: Dividends rise from $4.87 per share in the base case to $5.79 by 2029. That is slower than the historical increase from $2.77 to $4.43, because dividends and buybacks already consumed 94.8% of FY2026 free cash flow. The bear freezes the current $1.19 quarterly rate at $4.76 annually. The bull reaches $6.14 by 2029 through increases near the recent 10% pace.

blocks.heading: What has Paychex guided for the year?

paragraphs.text: Paychex’s September 23, 2026 outlook for the year ending May 2027 calls for total revenue growth of 5.0%–6.0% and adjusted diluted earnings-per-share growth of 7.0%–9.0%. Revenue is what customers pay; earnings per share is the profit assigned to each share. “Adjusted” earnings exclude selected acquisition-related costs, including Paycor intangible-asset amortization, integration compensation and severance.

Paychex raised its PEO and Insurance Solutions growth outlook to 7.0%–8.0% and its client-fund interest outlook to $200.0 million–$210.0 million, but left its overall targets unchanged. Reported EPS was $1.21 against adjusted EPS of $1.34 in the first quarter of fiscal 2027. The important test is whether Paycor eventually creates enough revenue and efficiency to outweigh the real costs excluded from adjusted results.

blocks.heading: Has Paychex kept its past promises?

paragraphs.text: Paycor’s promised benefits provide the strongest test. Paychex’s January 2025 investor presentation promised annual cost savings above US$80 million, followed by an increase in adjusted earnings per share. Fiscal 2026 adjusted earnings per share reached US$5.51, up 11%, but company-wide growth cannot prove the acquisition’s separate contribution. The real question is whether Paycor’s technology, recruiting capabilities and customer relationships produce durable gains after integration. The evidence so far suggests alignment between leaders and shareholders, but not yet a completed case that management has earned their trust.

blocks.heading: What do Paychex's last eight quarters show?

paragraphs.text: This quarter gives a cleaner view because both periods contained a full quarter of Paycor. Management Solutions grew more slowly than PEO and Insurance Solutions, while client-fund interest also helped revenue. That mix shows growth inside the combined business, not merely the mathematical effect of an acquisition.

blocks.heading: What should Paychex investors watch next?

paragraphs.text: The next quarterly report should clarify whether underlying demand is strengthening. Management expects second-quarter revenue growth of about 4%, partly because the prior year included acquisition-related revenue benefits and investment gains. WISE Hire’s October 20–22 demonstration at the HR Technology Conference matters less than subsequent adoption and revenue.
